name: Uvinul A Plus

lead: Uvinul A Plus is a UVA filter found in some sunscreens, particularly in Europe. It is described as photostable.
Sources are thin: chemistry papers and a 2020 human metabolism study, with no appearance trials.

paras: It absorbs UVA light, peaking near 354 nm, and dissipates the energy.
The EU safety committee flagged a manufacturing impurity (di-n-hexyl phthalate) and recommended limits. Human metabolism was studied after oral and dermal doses in 2020.

lead: Uvinul A Plus is BASF's trade name for diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, also sold as Parsol DHHB), an organic UVA-absorbing sunscreen filter. It is described as photostable and is used in sunscreens and other cosmetics in the European Union at up to 10 percent.[1][2][3]
Available research is chemical and toxicokinetic: a 2017 photophysics study and a 2020 human metabolism study. No trials of appearance outcomes were found.

paras: A 2017 photophysical study examined DHHB through transient absorption, emission, phosphorescence and electron paramagnetic resonance spectra, describing it as a photostable UVA absorber.[2] Wikipedia lists a maximum absorbance of 354 nm.[3]

Wikipedia states that the EU approved DHHB for sunscreens in 2005 at up to 10 percent, and that it is also approved in several countries including Japan and Mexico but is not a US sunscreen active.[3] The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety flagged possible contamination with di-n-hexyl phthalate from manufacturing and recommended limits on the impurity.[3]
A 2020 study gave volunteers a single oral or dermal dose and followed metabolism and urinary excretion over 72 hours, identifying metabolites with a new UHPLC-MS/MS method.[1]
A 2020 human study examined metabolism and urinary excretion after single oral and dermal exposure.[1] No studies of skin-appearance or photoprotection outcomes for this filter alone were found.
